name: Uzbek
variety: Standard Uzbek of Uzbekistan, based on the Tashkent dialect; Latin script (Cyrillic also in use)
sources: Ido, Shinji (2025). Uzbek. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 55(1-2), 152-168.
Sjoberg, Andrée F. (1963). Uzbek Structural Grammar. Indiana University.
Bodrogligeti, András J. E. (2003). An Academic Reference Grammar of Modern Literary Uzbek. Lincom Europa.
Boeschoten, Hendrik (1998). Uzbek. In Lars Johanson & Éva Á. Csató (eds.), The Turkic Languages. Routledge.

vowel_formants.speaker: adult male (one Tashkent speaker; only /o/ and /u/ are given as numbers, each the mean of two words, bo'l and uch)

contrasts: six vowels, without front rounded vowels and without front-back pairs: /i e a/ and /u o ɔ/, spelt i e a and u oʻ o
velar /k ɡ/ versus uvular /q ʁ χ/, not predictable from the vowels
/χ/ versus /h/ in careful standard speech (merged in traditional Tashkent speech)
vowel length only in loanwords (maʼno, maʼqul)
allophony: /i/ is a short, lax, centralised vowel in most words (biz, bir) and is closer and fronter next to palatal consonants; Ido (2025) treats the central variant as a separate seventh vowel that forms no minimal pairs with /i/
close vowels are often devoiced next to voiceless consonants or dropped in unstressed syllables (qishloq, kuchli)
/ɔ/ ranges between [ɑ] and a raised [ɔ], with variation between words, speakers and utterances
/o/ occurs almost only in root-initial syllables
/k ɡ/ are palatalised [kʲ ɡʲ] before non-back vowels and when released word-finally (kam [kʲam], kerak [kʲeɾakʲ])
voiceless plosives have a degree of aspiration
/ɾ/ does not begin native words; word-finally it is usually a trill and may be devoiced and fricated
the sibilants and affricates vary between alveolo-palatal [ɕ tɕ dʑ] and postalveolar [ʃ tʃ dʒ]; /dʒ/ is [ʒ] before a plosive (ajdar)
/f v/ are labiodental in the present standard, formerly bilabial [ɸ β]
a short vowel is inserted in clusters of a velar or uvular plosive plus a more front consonant (tegdi, yoqdi)
/ʔ/ occurs in a few Arabic loans; a non-phonemic glottal stop may precede a word-initial vowel at a phrase boundary
phonotactics: no onset clusters in native words; Russian loans keep theirs (plash)
coda clusters occur in native stems and loans (toʻrt, qirq, xalq, fasl), some with an epenthetic vowel
very little vowel harmony: suffixes have one fixed form (-lar, -da, -ning); only a few vestiges remain

stress.type: fixed final by default, with morphological and lexical exceptions
stress.rule: Primary stress falls on the last syllable; certain suffixes and enclitics repel it, and some proper names, loanwords and question words (qaysi) have non-final stress.
stress.cues: the vowel of the final syllable is lengthened, while F0 and intensity are highest on the penultimate syllable (Ido 2025)

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: close vowels are centralised, devoiced or dropped in unstressed syllables; the other vowels keep their quality

length.notes: Vowel length is not phonological in native words of Tashkent and standard Uzbek; lengthened vowels occur in some Arabic and Persian loans, often spelt with the tutuq belgisi (maʼno). Geminates occur in numerals and loans (ikki, yetti, toʻqqiz).

intonation.declarative: rise towards the end of non-final words and phrases, fall at the end of the statement
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by the enclitic -mi; pitch is high before the enclitic
intonation.wh_question: prominence on the question word, final fall
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of non-final phrases
intonation.accent_shape: F0 peak on the penultimate syllable with lengthening of the final syllable in citation forms (Ido 2025)
intonation.notes: Sentence intonation is low confidence: Ido (2025) analysed citation forms only, and the sentence entries follow the general pattern of the better described Turkic languages.

phonation: devoiced close vowels next to voiceless consonants

problems: the letter i is mapped to the phoneme y, imported from base2 as the front rounded vowel [y] (F2 about 1720 Hz), so every i sounds like ü (kitob gives [kytɑb], qiz gives [qyz])
no stress rule is set for uz, so the default penultimate stress applies (bola, kitob, vatan are stressed on the first syllable); Uzbek stress is final
numbers are switched off in the language options, so digits are read one by one
the tutuq belgisi ʼ (U+02BC, also produced from Cyrillic ь and ъ) has no rule: a word such as maʼno is spelt out letter by letter
the rule for f gives 'f,' and so puts a secondary stress mark on the following vowel (fasl)
no centralised or devoiced variants of /i/ and /u/, no palatalisation of /k ɡ/, no lengthened vowels in loans
t is the unaspirated base2 stop while p and k use aspirated samples
good: q, x and gʻ are uvular [q χ ʁ]; ng is [ŋ]
o is a rounded open back vowel and oʻ is [o]
Latin and Cyrillic spelling are both accepted

notes: The voice is marked 'status testing' in eSpeak NG. Front rounded vowels exist in many dialects but not in Tashkent or standard Uzbek (Ido 2025).
